item.research_question: How do atomic interactions and Ti content influence the order–disorder transition and phase stability in FCC-type FeCoNiAl1−xTix high-entropy alloys?
item.material_system: FeCoNiAl1−xTix (specifically Fe25Co25Ni25Al25−xTix) with Ti content ranging from 0 to 9 at.%
item.processing_route: First-principles calculations using DFT (VASP, PAW method, PBE functional, 500 eV plane waves, 3×3×3 supercells) to determine atomic interactions; Thermodynamic Monte Carlo simulations (62,500 atoms, 2300 K to 300 K, 4000 steps equilibration); CALPHAD simulations using Thermo-Calc 2021b with TCHEA5 database and Sheil–Gulliver model.
item.test_conditions: Simulated temperatures from 2300 K down to 300 K; Ti concentrations of 0, 1, 3, 5, and 7 at.% (replacing Al); ferromagnetic state for Ni, Fe, Co.
key_findings: The order–disorder transition temperature for equal-atomic AlCoFeNi HEAs was calculated at 1650 K.
The order–disorder transition temperature decreased with increasing Ti content: 1644 K (1 at.% Ti), 1638 K (3 at.% Ti), 1632 K (5 at.% Ti), and 1574 K (7 at.% Ti).
CALPHAD predicted L12 precipitation temperatures of 1600 K, 1540 K, 1490 K, and 1465 K for alloys with 1, 3, 5, and 7 at.% Ti, respectively.
Ni3Al and Ni3Ti were identified as the most stable L12 intermetallics with formation enthalpies of −0.44 eV and −0.47 eV, respectively.
Co atoms accumulate and segregate at the interfaces of precipitates due to weak Co–Co atomic interactions (less than 0.03 eV).
Strain-induced interactions are significant for Al–X pairs due to the small atomic radius of Al (1.25 Å).
Laves phase precipitation was predicted to begin at approximately 1300 K when Ti content is large enough.
The simulated precipitate sizes in AlCoFeNi HEAs were found to be not greater than 35 nm.
item.mechanism: Atomic ordering is driven by repulsive nearest-neighbor interactions and strong strain-induced interactions caused by atomic size mismatch, particularly involving Al. The formation of L12 precipitates (Ni3Al, Ni3Ti, Fe3Al) is governed by the negative formation enthalpies of these intermetallics. Ti addition stabilizes the L12 phase thermodynamically but lowers the transition temperature, while Co atoms segregate at interfaces due to negligible interaction energies with other species.
item.limitations: The authors state that 'some disagreements between the CALPHAD simulated results based on the current databases and Monte Carlo as well as experimental results are still present' and that 'the severe lattice distortion caused by Ti alloying significantly changed the atomic configuration, which is a sensitive parameter for Monte Carlo simulations'. They also note that 'the order–disorder transition in FeCoNiAl1−xTix HEAs is complicated' involving site occupation and phase competition not fully covered.
item.future_work: The authors propose that 'the modulation of the Ti content would be an effective way to affect the microstructure and mechanical properties' and suggest that 'an investigation into the higher Ti content... would be an interesting subject for future investigations'. They also state that 'the site occupation in the L12 phase was found to be complex, and it requires further study'.
quotes: The order–disorder transition temperatures decrease with increasing Ti content in FeCoNiAl1−xTix high-entropy alloys
The order–disorder transition temperature decreased smoothly with the concentration of Ti in the Fe25Co25Ni25Al25−xTix HEAs in the range of 0–5 Ti at.%
Co atoms were found to accumulate at the interfaces between precipitates and matrix due to their weak interaction in FeCoNiAl1−xTix
